# Tree-based thinking

We have so far focused on learning how to construct _slendr_ demographic models,
how to compute summary statistics, and how exploratory, simulation-based
workflows help us study the behavior and limitations of those statistics.

In this chapter, we will change the pace a bit, and play with _slendr_ as a bit
of an "interactive popgen calculator" to quickly explore theoretical concepts in
a hands-on practical way, and build intuition into how (and why) they work the
way they do. We will also dig a little bit more into the tree-sequence data
itself.

Our main focus will be on $f$-statistics, mostly because they form such a
crucial component of population genomics research, specifically within the aDNA
context, and because they showcase very nicely why simulation-based exploration
can be so powerful. In the process, we will also learn a few useful _slendr_
tricks which are applicable for many other research problems.









## Exercise: "Outgroup" $f_3$ as a measure of overlap of tree paths

To ease into the problem of interpreting $f$-statistics as measures of
overlapping paths in "population trees" (or, when admixture comes into the
picture), in "population graphs", let's get back to our familiar $f_3$
statistic.

**Create a new script `fstatistics.R` and paste the following code into that
script. As always, read through the code, try to decipher what it's going to do,
run it and compare your understanding with the visualization of the model.**

```{r}
#| output: false
library(slendr)
init_env()

p4 <- population("p4", time = 20000, N = 1000)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1000, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1000, parent = p2)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), generation_time = 1)

schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 10))

plot_model(model, schedule = schedule)

ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
```

---

Now, consider the model from this script:

```{r}
#| echo: false
plot_model(model, schedule = schedule)
```

We know from [the theory of
$f$-statistics](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/202/4/1485/5930214)
that:

- $f_2(A, B)$ statistic measures the branch length between two samples A
and B (two individuals, two groups of individuals, etc.), and

- similarly, $f_3(C; A, B)$ statistic is formally defined as the branch length
which connects the internal most recent common ancestor node of A and B with the
sample C.

This can be seen graphically in Figure 1 of that linked paper.

Another thing established in the paper is the fact that any $f$-statistic can be
expressed as a linear combination of $f_2$ statistics. If you're not familiar
with linear algebra, this might sound a bit obscure. More concretely, for
instance, equation (20b) in the same paper states the following, which
decomposes an $f_3$ statistic into a composite of simpler $f_2$ statistics (this
is what "linear combination" basically is):

$$f_3(A; B, C) = \frac{1}{2} (f_2(A, C) + f_2(A, B) - f_2(B, C))$$

---

**Draw a sketch of the population model plotted above on a piece of paper, then
trace by hand the paths indicated by the three $f_2$ statistics in this equation
on that drawn model (again, knowing that $f_2(x, y)$ indicates the length of the
path from ($x$ to $y$), let's say substituting A = p4, B = p1, C = p2. When you
add up and subtract the paths from each other (graphically, on your drawn
model), do you arrive at the definition of "outgroup" $f_3$ as a measure
of shared branch between B and C towards the outgroup A?**


---


True story: When I was writing this chapter, I made a mistake in the equation
above, and wrote a quick simulation to double-check that the equation is
correct. This is the true motivation for this little exercise, showing why
simulations are also helpful!

**Now let's move to R. Use the function `ts_f2()` to implement this equation in
code, computing a "homemade" $f_3(A = p4; B = p1, C = p2)$ statistic which you
just solved on paper, and compare it to the result produced by `ts_f3()`
provided by _slendr_. Do you get the same result?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

First let's get our groups of individuals in the tree sequence:

```{r}
s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
s
```

Now let's compute $f_3$ using the built-in _slendr_ function:

```{r}
simulated_f3 <- ts_f3(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p1"], C = s["p2"])
simulated_f3
```

And now let's compose a "homemade" $f_3$ statistic as a linear combination of
$f_2$ statistics as given by the equation:

```{r}
homemade_f3 <- 1/2 * (
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p1"])$f2 +
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p2"])$f2 -
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p1"], B = s["p2"])$f2
)
homemade_f3
```

You can see that the `ts_f3()` implementation gives basically the same value as
our "homemade" implementation based on a linear combination of $f_2$ statistics,
just as predicted by the underlying math!

:::









## Exercise: Mutations versus branches

Do you recall how I told you earlier that you don't have to add mutations to
your tree sequence `ts`, and still be able to compute population genetic
statistics? But that you can safely add them with `ts_mutate()` anyway?

The reason this works is because some very smart people figured out a
mathematical [duality between mutation-based and branch-based
statistics](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/215/3/779/5930459)---it
actually doesn't matter which way we compute our statistics, they give
mathematically the same result in terms of theoretical statistical expectations
(i.e., expectations of what happen in real data).

**Try to repeat the previous task, but this time specify `mode = "branch"` in
all your `ts_f3()` and `ts_f2()` commands. Feel free to make a copy of your
`ts_f3()` and `ts_f2()`-based code in your `f_null.R` script and and modify
the copies for easier comparison. What numbers do you get compared to the
results of the previous exercise? Can you relate those numbers to what your
population tree model visualization indicates (in terms of branch lenghts)? Look
at your sketch with pen and paper again if this helps.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

```{r}
ts_f3(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p1"], C = s["p2"], mode = "branch")
```

```{r}
homemade_f3 <- (
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p1"], mode = "branch")$f2 +
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p2"], mode = "branch")$f2 -
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p1"], B = s["p2"], mode = "branch")$f2
) / 2

homemade_f3
```

We can see that when we use the `"branch"` mode of operation, the returned
values of $f$ statistics correspond to the _real branch lengths_ in terms of
times! Which is quite cool because as we discussed, the mathematical expectation
of $f$ statistics does, after all, represent tree path overlap going from p1
and p2 to the "outgroup" p4:

```{r}
#| echo: false
plot_model(model)
```

:::


Hopefully, you can now appreciate that there's nothing magical about $f$
statistics. Even though their practical interpretation can get sometimes
complicated, internally they _always_ boil down to tracing paths through
population trees in order to obtain statistical expectations of allele frequency
correlations between lineages under study, easily visualized by tracing paths
through population trees.

In a way, setting `mode = "branch"` can be understood as instructing _slendr_ to
compute the results --- in this case, of the $f_3$ statistic --- in "real time
units", generations.











## Exercise: Basic intuition into the $f_4$ statistic

Now let's finally dig into exploring perhaps the most critical component of
population genetics research (particularly in the context of ancient DNA
genomics)---the venerable $f_4$-statistic, formally established by Nick
Patterson and David Reich in 2008.

From the [intuitive follow-up paper on $f$-statistics by Benjamin
Peter](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/202/4/1485/5930214), we know
that (in a very similar way to $f_2$ and $f_3$), the $f_4(W, X; Y, Z)$ statistic
can be interpreted as quantifying the overlap between the paths in a tree
connecting W-X and Y-Z pairs of lineages, as is demonstrated in Figure 1 of the
linked paper.

That said, what value does any given $f_4$ statistic _actually_ gives you of
course depends on the (in practice, hidden) underlying demographic model which
determines how populations are related and also what do we assign into each of
the four positions of that $f_4$ "quartet configuration".

---

**Given the phylogenetic relationships between the populations encoded by the
model in `f_null.R`, what value would you expect for $f_4(p1, p2; p3, p4)$?
try to guess first without any coding simply by taking a look at the sketch of
your model again tracing the path overlaps between p1-p2 and p3-p4, then compute
the statistic on a `ts` simulated data with the `ts_f4()` function. Does your
simulation give you the _exact_ result you might expect based on the
visualization of the model alone? If it doesn't give you the exact expected
result, why could this be?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### click to see the solution

As we can see below, $f$-statistics theory tells us that the value should be
zero, but without any reference point, we get a number which is very tiny (the
value in the `f4` column), but how tiny would it have to be to be "basically
zero"?

```{r}
ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p2"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"])
```

The reason we didn't get _exactly_ zero is stochastic noise of any evolutionary
process, which means that that along a genome (even a small one, only 10 Mb of
simulated sequence) there are many possible trees. Sometimes, [incomplete
lineage sorting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incomplete_lineage_sorting) will
lead to genealogical trees which do not fit the tidy, well-behaved population
tree like the one we see when we run `plot_model()`.

That said, gene trees that don't fit the overall population trees will tend to
"average out", particularly when we look across many different regions of the
genome.

:::

---

As suggested in the solution above, the reason we don't get a perfectly zero
expected value of the $f_4$ is because of ILS and stochasticity. Let's test this
hypothesis now.

**First, evaluate `ts` in your R console and note how many individual trees do you
have in your 10 Mb tree-sequence.**

**Now, restart your R session (`Session -> Restart R`). Then, temporarily change
the $N_e$ of all lineages in your model to 1 and re-run your script to get a new
`ts` and compute the same $f_4$ statistic again. $N_e$ of one implies
ridiculously high amount of drift, which should eliminate ILS completely, giving
us $f_4$ close to its mathematical expectation of zero. Is this true? How many
trees does your tree sequence have now?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

```{r}
#| echo: false
ts_num_trees <- ts$num_trees
```

We changed all N sizes to 1, then we rerun the entire script `f_statistics.R`
again:

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

#
# !!!
# note the (temporary) change to N = 1
# !!!
#
p4 <- population("p4", time = 20000, N = 1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1, parent = p2)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), generation_time = 1)

ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
```

Now let's compute the $f_4$ again on the `ts` tree sequence produced by this
extreme model:

```{r}
ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p2"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"])
```

Indeed, when we type `ts` into the R console, we see that it only contains `{r}
ts$num_trees` individual trees compared to the previous count of `{r}
ts_num_trees`, consistent with an absolutely extreme amounts of genetic drift in
your model.

:::

---

Of course, changing $N_e$ to value of 1 as we did above is a drastic measure of
generally only theoretical utility. We could hardly get away with doing that, if
we wanted to use simulations to make a point in our research paper.

How do we deal with the unavoidable stochasticity in our simulations then? This
wasn't much of a problem in exercises in the previous chapters, but we need the
way to solve this to be able to get useful, applicable results.

Let's look into this now.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

```{r}
#| echo: false
p4 <- population("p4", time = 20000, N = 1000)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1000, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1000, parent = p2)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), generation_time = 1)

ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
```

:::






## Exercise: Reducing stochastic noise via simulation replicates

As a means to tame the stochasticity and help meaningful statistical patterns
stand out, I recently implemented a new _slendr_ function `ts_replicates()`,
specifically for this workshop! The way it works is like this:

```{r}
#| eval: false
ts_replicate(
  n = <number of replicates>,
  {
    # ...
    # a block of slendr code wrapped in { ... } containing a ts simulation
    # and a slendr statistical computation we want to run in replicates
    # ...
  }
)
```

---

**Take a look at its manual page under `?ts_replicates`, then use it to run 10
replicate simulations of the $f_4$ statistic above** (the one which should give
us a zero expectation, but it wasn't clear if it did or not), **saving it to
variable `df`. What format does the result have? When you visualize the
distribution of $f_4$ values across all replicates, are they more understandable
in terms of the statistical expectation for this particular $f_4$ quartet?**

::: aside

**Note:** If you want to speed up the replicate simulation, not that
`?ts_replicate` describes the means to run multiple simulations in parallel.

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Here's how we can tweak the "template" above to answer the question:

```{r}
df <- ts_replicate(
  n = 10, {
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

  ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p2"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"])
})
```

We can see that we get the same format of the data frame as normally produced by
the `ts_f4()` function, except with a new column `rep` added, indicating a
replicate number.

```{r}
df
```

This means we can visualize their distribution easily like this, for example:

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(df, aes(statistic, f4)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed")
```

As we can see, when we run multiple replicates of the simulation, we are able to
"control" the stochastic noise a bit, making the expected pattern stand out more
clearly: we see that the expected value of `{r} unique(df$statistic)` is really
zero (up to that unavoidable stochastic noise).

:::

## Exercise: Other $f_4$ "quartets"

Of course, $f_4(p1, p2; p3, p4)$ is only one possible "quartet configuration".

**Expand your 10 replicates simulation $f_4(p1, p2; p3, p4)$ by adding the
computation of $f_4(p1, p3; p2, p4)$ and $f_4(p1, p4; p2, p3)$ in the same
`{...}` block provided to `ts_replicate()` (making sure you bind all three data
resulting frames together at the end)..**

**How would you compare the interpretation of the three $f_4$ statistics,
looking at your sketch of the four-population model (or by looking at the
visualization of the model below), before running and visualizing the expanded
replication code you just wrote? Does your interpretation fit what you get from
the simulation once you run it?**


::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Let's add the computation of all three $f_4$ statistics in the same replicate
simulation pipeline:

```{r}
df <- ts_replicate(
  n = 10, {
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

  rbind(
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p2"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"]), # 1st f4
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p3"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p4"]), # 2nd f4
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p3"])  # 3rd f4
  )
})
```

We get a data frame with multiple replicates for each of the three statistics:

```{r}
df
```

From the mathematical definition of $f_4$ as internal branch lengths between two
pairs of lineages in a given "quartet" and knowing the topological structure of
our population tree, we can predict that the first $f_4$ is expected to be zero
(which is what we established earlier), and the other two $f_4$ statistics are
expected to have the same value corresponding to the internal branch length
connecting pairs p1-p2 and p3-p4.

This is exactly what we see in our results:

```{r}
ggplot(df, aes(statistic, f4)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed")
```

:::

---

**Make a copy of your `ts_replicate()` code and modify it by setting `mode =
"branch"`, as we did before for the example $f_3$ simulation. As mentioned
above, this instructs _slendr_'s internal statistical machinery to effectively
use "model time units" (here, generations) in computing the results. When you
visualize the three $f_4$ statistics computed in this way, do you see this being
the case?**


::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Let's save the result in a new data frame `df_branch`:

```{r}
df_branch <- ts_replicate(
  n = 10, {
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

  rbind(
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p2"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"], mode = "branch"), # 1st f4
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p3"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p4"], mode = "branch"), # 2nd f4
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p3"], mode = "branch")  # 3rd f4
  )
})
```

When we visualize the results, we do indeed see that the `f4` column contains
the expected branch lengths expressed in real generation times! Here are the
results plotted alongside the model using the package _cowplot_ (from which the
branch length times can be read more easily):

```{r}
library(cowplot) # get access to the plot_grid() function

plot_grid(
  # first panel:
  plot_model(model, schedule = schedule),

  # second panel:
  ggplot(df_branch, aes(statistic, f4)) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    geom_jitter() +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed"),

  # plot both panels in two rows:
  nrow = 2
)
```

:::










## Catch up

This was a lot of work! If you want to check in with the state of our
$f$-statistics exploratory simulation script `f_null.R`, here it is in the form
which showcases the most important results from this chapter so far:

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the entire script

```{r}
##################################################
# load the necessary packages

library(ggplot2)
library(cowplot)

library(slendr)
init_env()

##################################################
# define the basic structure of our demographic model

p4 <- population("p4", time = 20000, N = 1000)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1000, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1000, parent = p2)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), generation_time = 1)

schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 10))

##################################################
# simulate replicates of the three f4 statistics
# (based on branches)

df <- ts_replicate(
  n = 10, {
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

  rbind(
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p2"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"], mode = "branch"),
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p3"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p4"], mode = "branch"),
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p3"], mode = "branch")
  )
})

##################################################
# visualize branch-based f4 statistics alongside
# the corresponding demographic model

p_df <- ggplot(df, aes(statistic, f4)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed")

p_model <- plot_model(model, schedule = schedule)

p_panels <- plot_grid(p_model, p_df, nrow = 2)

p_panels
```

:::











## Exercise: Interpreting $f_4$ as an admixture hypothesis test

Admittedly, thinking about $f$ statistics as measures of allele frequency
correlations between populations and interpreting them as overlapping branch
lengths is intellectually interesting in terms of population genetics theory (at
least if you're a nerd like me!), but in practice, they are most famous as
admixture tests.

**Create a new script `f_admixture.R` and copy my solutions to the exercises in
this chapter available under the _"Catch up"_ section into that script. Restart
your R session (`Session -> Restart R`) then skim through this script and re-run
it all. Having gone through the exercises, the code should look somewhat
familiar and the visualization you obtain by typing out `p_panels` into your R
console (the branch lengths encoded by the three $f_4$ statistics we studied)
should make sense.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Here's the final visualization of the three $f_3$ statistics for easier
reference as you work on the following exercise.

```{r}
#| echo: false
p_panel
```

:::


---

**Introduce the following two changes to the `f_admixture.R` script:**

1. **Program a `gene_flow()` event `gf`, introducing 10% gene-flow from p3 to p2
between 500 and 400 generations ago.**

2. **Add this `gf` event into the `model` compilation step, making sure it's
included in the demographic model.**

**With the steps 1. and 2. done, you're model now includes admixture. Re-run the
script again, and inspect the final visualization obtained by typing out
`p_panels` into your R console.**

**How does admixture from p3 to p2 affect the branch lengths compared to the
previous model `f_null.R`, which (as the name indicates) represented a null
model of no admixture? Pay particular attention to the $f_4(p1,p2;p3,p4)$
statistic which had an expected value of zero---does it still have a zero
value?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Here's only the final visualization of the figure in the `p_panel` variable:

```{r}
#| echo: false
##################################################
# load the necessary packages

library(ggplot2)
library(cowplot)

library(slendr)
init_env()

##################################################
# define the basic structure of our demographic model

p4 <- population("p4", time = 20000, N = 1000)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1000, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1000, parent = p2)

gf <- gene_flow(from = p3, to = p2, start = 500, end = 400, proportion = 0.1)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), gene_flow = gf, generation_time = 1)

schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 10))

##################################################
# simulate replicates of the three f4 statistics
# (based on branches)

df <- ts_replicate(
  n = 10, {
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

  rbind(
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p2"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"], mode = "branch"),
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p3"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p4"], mode = "branch"),
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p3"], mode = "branch")
  )
})

##################################################
# visualize branch-based f4 statistics alongside
# the corresponding demographic model

p_df <- ggplot(df, aes(statistic, f4)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed")

p_model <- plot_model(model, schedule = schedule)

p_panels <- plot_grid(p_model, p_df, nrow = 2)

p_panels
```

As we can see, because of the admixture event, our previously tree-like
population model is no longer tree. In the tree model without an admixture edge,
there was no path overlap between the pairs p1-p2 and p3-p4, which is why the
$f_4(p1,p2;p3,p4)$ statistic was zero.

Admixture is a violation of "treeness", because "mathematical" trees are not
allowed to have admixture edges---structures which do have edges are called
"admixture graphs", This is why the statistic now significantly deviates from
zero.

This is exactly why $f_4(p1,p2;p3,p4)$ serves as a statistical hypothesis test
of admixture.

:::








## Exercise: Estimating admixture proportions

From the little simulation and tree-doodling experiments above we now got a
sense of how various $f$ statistics (and particularly $f_4$ statistics)
mathematically quantify allele frequency correlations between lineages of
population trees and how they can be interpreted as the amounts of overlaps of
paths traced along branches of those trees. We also got an idea how different
patterns emerge in $f_4$ statistic expectation when gene-flow is introduced into
population trees, adding admixture edges to them and turning them into so-called
"admixture graphs".

It turns out that the same principles allow us to not just test the hypothesis
of whether an admixture event happened in the history of our samples, but also
estimate the proportion of ancestry derived from admixture.

```{r}
ts <-
msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

x <- ts_f4(ts, W = "p3_1", X = s["p4"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p1"])$f4 / 
ts_f4(ts, W = "p3_1", X = s["p4"], Y = "p3_2", Z = s["p1"])$f4
x

y <- ts_f4(ts, W = "p3_1", X = s["p4"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p1"])$f4 / 
ts_f4(ts, W = "p3_1", X = s["p4"], Y = "p3_2", Z = s["p1"])$f4
y
```



```{r}
ts_replicate(20, {
ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 30e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
  
x <- ts_f4(ts, W = "p3_1", X = s["p4"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p1"])$f4 / 
  ts_f4(ts, W = "p3_1", X = s["p4"], Y = "p3_2", Z = s["p1"])$f4

y <- ts_f4(ts, W = "p3_1", X = s["p4"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p1"])$f4 / 
  ts_f4(ts, W = "p3_1", X = s["p4"], Y = "p3_2", Z = s["p1"])$f4

# ts_f4(ts, A, O, X[i], C, mode = mode)$f4 /
# ts_f4(ts, A, O, B, C, mode = mode)$f4

ts_f4ratio(ts, "p2_1", A = "p3_1", B = "p3_2", C = s["p1"], O = s["p4"]) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(x = x, y = y)
}, parallel = 10) -> df

df

plot_grid(
  plot_model(model), 
  ggplot() +
    geom_density(data = df, aes(alpha), color = "red") +
    geom_density(data = df, aes(x), color = "blue") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = c(0, 0.1)) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 0.5)),
  nrow = 2
)

mean(df$alpha)
mean(df$x)
```









## Exercise: Masking evidence of admixture?

In another amazing [follow-up
paper](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11563031/) on $f$ statistics and
admixture graphs which provides advice and guidance on performing admixture analyses,
the author writes the following:

> two admixture events together can cause an $f_4$-statistic to be close to zero
and thereby mask the signal of admixture

Obviously, this can be a rather worrisome, because real-world population histories
are very complex and involve, of course, multiple admixture events across our idealized population trees.

**Try to modify your admixture model by introducing such second gene-flow event,
which would make the $f_4(p1,p2;p3,p4)$ statistic (which we established serves
as an admixture test) return back to a near-zero expectation, and therefore mask
evidence of p3-p2 admixture even though we know it happened in the simulation.**
